title: Arrays and lists
summary: An ordered row of values you can read by position, grow, and loop over.

sections.heading: A numbered row of values
body: An array (a list in Python) keeps values in order. Each one has a position called an index, and counting starts at 0, not 1.
So the last item is at `length - 1`. Python also lets you count from the end with `-1`.

typescript.code:
const fruits: string[] = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
console.log(fruits[0])
console.log(fruits.length)
console.log(fruits[fruits.length - 1])

sections.heading: Building a new list in a loop
body: A very common shape: start with an empty list, loop over the input, and add one result each time.
This leaves the input untouched, which is usually what tests expect.

python.code:
nums = [3, 1, 4]
doubled = []
for n in nums:
    doubled.append(n * 2)
print(doubled)

sections.heading: When you need the position too
body: Sometimes the index matters, for example "return the positions of...". Use a counting loop in JavaScript, or `enumerate` in Python, which gives you the index and the value together.

sections.heading: Carrying a value through the loop
body: Keep a variable outside the loop and update it on every step: a count, a total, the biggest value so far.
Think about where it starts. Starting a "largest" at `0` breaks when every number is negative; start from the first item instead.

mistakes: Looping with `i <= arr.length` goes one step too far. Use `<`.
Reading past the end gives `undefined` in JavaScript but raises `IndexError` in Python.
Adding or removing items from a list while you loop over it skips items. Build a new list instead.
